clinicalPearls: All parts of common oleander (Nerium oleander) and yellow oleander (Cascabela/Thevetia peruviana) contain cardiac glycosides such as oleandrin and thevetin that act like digoxin.
Yellow oleander seed ingestion is a common means of deliberate self-poisoning in parts of South Asia and can cause fatal cardiotoxicity.
Clinical picture combines gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain) with cardiac glycoside toxicity: bradyarrhythmias, varying degrees of heart block and ventricular ectopy.
Hyperkalaemia from inhibition of the sodium-potassium ATPase is a marker of severe acute poisoning and correlates with poor outcome, mirroring acute digoxin toxicity.
The glycosides inhibit the myocardial sodium-potassium pump, raising intracellular calcium and increasing vagal tone, which enhances automaticity while depressing conduction.
Smoke from burning the plant and even honey or water contaminated by it can transmit toxin; boiling and cooking do not render the plant safe.

Digoxin-specific antibody fragments can bind oleander glycosides and are the definitive treatment for life-threatening arrhythmia or hyperkalaemia, though larger amounts may be needed due to cross-reactivity differences.
Standard serum digoxin immunoassays may cross-react and give a positive but unreliable quantitative result, useful qualitatively to support the diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Oleander poisoning is caused by cardenolide cardiac glycosides, notably oleandrin in Nerium oleander and thevetin and related glycosides in yellow oleander, which are present throughout the plant including leaves, flowers, sap and seeds. Like digoxin these glycosides inhibit the membrane sodium-potassium ATPase of cardiac and other cells. Inhibition of the pump raises intracellular sodium, which reduces the driving force for the sodium-calcium exchanger and thereby increases intracellular calcium, augmenting myocardial contractility but also promoting delayed afterdepolarisations and increased automaticity. Simultaneously the glycosides enhance vagal tone and slow conduction through the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, producing the characteristic combination of increased ventricular ectopy with bradyarrhythmias and atrioventricular block. In acute poisoning, widespread inhibition of the sodium-potassium pump in skeletal muscle and other tissues causes efflux of potassium into the plasma, so that rising serum potassium reflects the severity of toxin effect and predicts adverse outcome. Gastrointestinal glycoside effects and mucosal irritation account for the early vomiting and diarrhoea. Because the toxins are heat-stable, cooking, boiling or burning does not eliminate the hazard.
additionalDifferentials: Digoxin or other medicinal cardiac glycoside toxicity
Other cardiac-glycoside-containing plants such as foxglove (Digitalis) or lily of the valley
Beta-blocker or calcium-channel-blocker overdose with bradycardia
Primary cardiac conduction disease or ischaemia
Hyperkalaemia from renal failure or other cause
additionalInvestigations: Continuous cardiac monitoring and serial 12-lead ECGs for bradyarrhythmia, heart block and ectopy
Serum potassium and other electrolytes, with potassium as a key severity marker
Serum digoxin immunoassay used qualitatively given cross-reactivity with oleander glycosides
Magnesium and calcium levels to guide arrhythmia management
Blood glucose and basic metabolic screen to exclude mimics
Identification of the plant, seeds or preparation ingested
redFlags: Rising serum potassium indicating severe glycoside effect
Deliberate ingestion of yellow oleander seeds
reference.prognosis: Many patients recover with monitoring and supportive care, but poisoning complicated by marked hyperkalaemia, high-grade heart block or ventricular arrhythmia carries a substantial mortality. Timely use of digoxin-specific antibody fragments and cardiac support improves survival in severe cases.
pitfalls: Relying on the quantitative serum digoxin level to gauge severity, as immunoassay cross-reactivity is only approximate
Giving calcium for hyperkalaemia as one might in other settings, which is generally avoided in cardiac glycoside toxicity
Assuming boiling, cooking or burning detoxifies the plant
Overlooking contaminated honey, water or smoke as sources of exposure
Failing to anticipate deterioration in an initially stable patient after seed ingestion
